content: The optimal target blood pressure for pregnant women with mild to moderate hypertension remains a topic of ongoing debate. This study aimed to compare the effects of tight versus very tight blood pressure control in pregnant women with mild to moderate pre-existing or non-proteinuric gestational hypertension to determine which approach yields better outcomes. To conduct this analysis, researchers searched multiple databases, including the Cochrane Pregnancy and Childbirth Group's Trials Register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, and the metaRegister of Controlled Trials, up to March 31, 2011. They also manually reviewed citation lists from relevant publications and included studies. Only randomized controlled trials comparing tight and very tight blood pressure control in this population were included. Two independent reviewers assessed the quality of the trials and extracted data. The results were expressed as risk ratios (RR) or mean differences (MD) with 95% confidence intervals (CI). The analysis included two studies involving a total of 256 participants with mild to moderate pre-existing or non-proteinuric gestational hypertension. The findings showed no significant difference between the tight and very tight control groups in the incidence of severe pre-eclampsia (RR 1.28, 95% CI 0.97 to 1.70). However, women in the tight control group were more likely to be hospitalized during pregnancy (RR 2.53, 95% CI 1.14 to 5.63; based on one trial with 125 participants). There was no evidence of significant differences between the two groups in other outcomes, including fetal distress, intrauterine growth restriction (IUGR), neonatal admission to a neonatal intensive care unit (NICU), perinatal deaths, induction of labor, or cesarean delivery. The mean difference in gestational age at delivery between the tight and very tight control groups was not statistically significant (MD -0.15 weeks, 95% CI -1.52 to 1.21; random-effects model, T² = 0.75, I² = 77%; two trials, 256 participants). Similarly, the mean difference in birthweight between the two groups was not significant (MD -100.00 grams, 95% CI -363.69 to 163.69; based on one trial with 125 participants). In conclusion, for pregnant women with mild to moderate pre-existing or non-proteinuric gestational hypertension, there is currently insufficient evidence to determine the optimal level of blood pressure control to improve maternal and fetal-neonatal outcomes. Further research is needed to clarify the best approach to managing blood pressure in this population.
